In 2017 the vault suffered a flood caused by a very warm winter combined with heavy spring rain to thaw part of the surrounding permafrost, flooding the entrance and threatening the safety of the seeds.  Changes have been made to the vault’s entrance to lessen this particular risk.

The timeline of the vault on the website of the vault’s partner, CropTrust, does not mention it. You don’t have to be a climate scientist to know the Arctic is losing permafrost; in Svalbard, the dislocation is obvious even to an untrained eye. And it’s long been known that the Arctic would warm more rapidly than the rest of the globe.

replies.author: @dorkski-k4y
replies.text: I was just there in July. Temperatures were about 8-10°C, sometimes dipping down to 5°C. It was quite mild, especially as much of Europe was over 35°C at the time. It's not particularly cold in summer and winters are getting shorter due to climate change. In order to leave Longyearbyen as a regular tourist you basically need to be on a guided tour per the polar bear regulations. One can do more adventurous/roughing it things, but there are also a lot of very comfortable tours by boat and automobile. One of the greatest goals there is to not see a polar bear. They mostly live in the northern parts but do wander south sometimes. Traveling there is not cheap. There are more affordable & rustic hostel-like accommodations, but most of the hotels are over 400€/night for a double room. The day tours can be 70€-350€ per person, depending on the type of trip, duration and what's included. Try to avoid travel companies run by the R*ssian state. Though there is relatively affordable alcohol at one shop if you A. do not live there, and B. did not arrive via cruise ship but rather by plane.
